title: Monetary Policy Report—October 2025
summary: The Bank of Canada's October 2025 Monetary Policy Report documents the Canadian economy adjusting to steep US tariffs, which have suppressed demand for Canadian goods and weighed on exports and business investment. CPI inflation stood at 2.4% in September, with total inflation near 2% and underlying inflation around 2.5%. The Bank cut its overnight policy rate by 25 basis points to 2.25% during this period. Projections show Canadian economic growth strengthening from roughly 0.75% in H2 2025 to average 1.4% annually over 2026-2027, with inflation expected to remain near the 2% target.
key_points: US tariffs have caused a fall in demand for Canadian goods and led to a slowdown in exports and business investment
CPI inflation was 2.4% in September 2025, with total inflation around 2% and underlying inflation approximately 2.5%
The Bank of Canada reduced its target overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.25% during this policy period
Canadian economic growth is projected to strengthen from approximately 0.75% in H2 2025 to average 1.4% annually over 2026-2027
Inflation is expected to remain near the 2% target over the projection horizon despite upward cost pressures from tariffs
Trade-related risks remain elevated, with the ongoing reconfiguration of global trade putting upward pressure on business input costs
why_it_matters: This Bank of Canada quarterly report provides the official institutional assessment of Canada's economic outlook amid significant trade disruptions from US tariffs. The combination of growth slowdown, near-target inflation, and a recent 25 bps rate cut signals the Bank's balanced response to tariff-related economic headwinds without abandoning its inflation mandate. Market participants monitoring Canadian dollar dynamics, Bank of Canada policy trajectory, and cross-border trade implications will find this essential reading.
macro_context: The report highlights a classic stagflationary tariff shock: elevated uncertainty and weaker demand weighing on growth while simultaneously pushing up costs through supply chain reconfiguration. The Bank projects these competing forces will roughly offset, keeping inflation near 2% while growth recovers modestly. The global context notes US tariffs are also pushing up inflation in the United States while weighing on global growth prospects.
